subsections: Drugs Used in CKD / Renal Replacement
Drugs Commonly Implicated in Specific Conditions

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do ACE inhibitors (e.g. ramipril) lower blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block angiotensin-converting enzyme, so less angiotensin II is made. This causes arteriolar vasodilation and less aldosterone (so sodium and water are lost), lowering BP and reducing cardiac afterload.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the main indications for ACE inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypertension (first-line if under 55 and not of Black African/Caribbean origin), heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (improves survival), post-MI secondary prevention, and diabetic nephropathy / proteinuric CKD.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Where do ACE inhibitors sit in NICE hypertension treatment, and what is the exception?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: First-line (an 'A' drug) if under 55 and not of Black African/Caribbean origin, and first-line at any age in type 2 diabetes for renoprotection. In Black African/Caribbean patients needing an A-drug, prefer an ARB.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical dose of ramipril?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ramipril 1.25-10 mg once daily, started low and titrated up (in heart failure, titrate to the maximum tolerated dose).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key contraindications to ACE inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Pregnancy (teratogenic - fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios), bilateral renal artery stenosis (precipitates AKI), and previous ACEi-induced angioedema (never re-challenge).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why are ACE inhibitors contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: These kidneys depend on angiotensin II to maintain GFR (efferent arteriole constriction). Blocking it drops filtration pressure and precipitates acute kidney injury.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What should you do if a patient on an ACE inhibitor develops a dry cough?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: The cough is caused by reduced bradykinin breakdown and affects ~15%. If intolerable, switch to an ARB - same benefits without the bradykinin effect, so the cough settles.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the important side effects of ACE inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dry cough, first-dose hypotension, hyperkalaemia, a rise in creatinine, and angioedema (an airway emergency, commoner in Black patients - never restart). Also taste disturbance.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How should a rising creatinine be interpreted after starting an ACE inhibitor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A rise of up to 30% (with K+ up to 5.5) is expected and acceptable - do not stop. A bigger jump suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis: stop and investigate.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring is required for ACE inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es before starting, at 1-2 weeks, and after every dose increase - to catch a large creatinine rise (renal artery stenosis) and hyperkalaemia early. Also monitor BP for response and postural drop.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why do NSAIDs plus an ACE inhibitor (and a diuretic) risk AKI?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole while the ACEi dilates the efferent arteriole, so glomerular filtration pressure collapses. This 'triple whammy' with a diuretic causes AKI - avoid or monitor U&Es and keep hydrated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs cause dangerous hyperkalaemia when combined with an ACE inhibitor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Other potassium-raising drugs: ARBs, spironolactone/eplerenone, amiloride, trimethoprim and K+ supplements. Do not routinely combine ACEi + ARB, and check K+ after adding an aldosterone antagonist.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the ACE inhibitor 'sick-day rule'?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hold the ACE inhibitor during any dehydrating illness (vomiting, diarrhoea, sepsis) and recheck U&Es, because of the risk of AKI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs (angiotensin receptor blockers): how do they lower blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the angiotensin II AT1 receptor, causing vasodilation and reduced aldosterone (like an ACEi), but without raising bradykinin, so they do not cause a dry cough.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: what are the main indications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypertension (same first-line niche as ACEi: under 55 or type 2 diabetes), heart failure with reduced EF (alternative to ACEi), and diabetic nephropathy / proteinuric CKD (renoprotective).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: when are they used instead of an ACEi?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: When an ACEi caused a troublesome dry cough (same benefits, no bradykinin), and as the preferred A-drug in Black African/Caribbean patients (including those with type 2 diabetes) per NICE.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: what are the key contraindications and cautions?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic) and bilateral renal artery stenosis (precipitates AKI). Caution in volume depletion, baseline K+ >5.0, and severe aortic stenosis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: what are the important side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia, rising creatinine, first-dose hypotension and dizziness. Unlike ACEi they do not cause cough, and angioedema is rare.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drug interactions with ARBs are dangerous?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: NSAIDs (additive AKI risk, 'triple whammy' with a diuretic), K+-raising drugs (spironolactone, trimethoprim, K+ supplements) causing hyperkalaemia, and lithium (reduced excretion -> toxicity). Never combine an ARB with an ACEi.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: what monitoring is required?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es before starting, at 1-2 weeks, and after each dose increase, to catch hyperkalaemia or a big creatinine rise (a rise >30% suggests renal artery stenosis; a rise up to 30% is acceptable). Hold in dehydrating illness (sick-day rule).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: ARBs: give a typical starting dose of a first-line agent.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Losartan 50 mg once daily (up to 100 mg). Candesartan 8 mg once daily (up to 32 mg) is another common choice.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g. amlodipine) lower blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block L-type Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle, causing arteriolar vasodilation and reducing BP. Dihydropyridines are vascular-selective, with little effect on heart rate or contractility.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Where do dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine) sit in the NICE hypertension pathway?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: First-line (step 1) for patients aged 55 or over, or of Black African/Caribbean origin at any age, in either case without type 2 diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the main indications for dihydropyridine CCBs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypertension and angina (via afterload reduction and coronary vasodilation). Nimodipine is used specifically to prevent cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical starting dose of amlodipine for hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 5 mg once daily, increased to 10 mg if needed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the classic side effect of dihydropyridine CCBs, and how should it be managed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ankle/peripheral oedema - very common and dose-related, caused by precapillary (arteriolar) dilation, NOT fluid overload. Diuretics don't help; reduce the dose or add an ACEi/ARB.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What other common side effects do dihydropyridine CCBs cause?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Flushing, headache and palpitations (reflex tachycardia), and gum hypertrophy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key cautions/contraindications for dihydropyridine CCBs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Caution in severe aortic stenosis (vasodilation can cause collapse), unstable angina and marked ankle oedema. Avoid in cardiogenic shock. Amlodipine is the safest CCB in stable heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which interactions matter with dihydropyridine CCBs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Grapefruit juice raises CCB blood levels and can cause hypotension (especially with felodipine). Amlodipine raises simvastatin levels, so cap simvastatin at 20 mg.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Key exam pearls for dihydropyridine CCBs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Amlodipine ankle oedema is vasodilation, not fluid, so don't give a diuretic. Nimodipine = subarachnoid haemorrhage, not blood pressure. Amlodipine is the CCB safe in stable heart failure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do rate-limiting (non-dihydropyridine) calcium channel blockers like verapamil and diltiazem lower BP and affect the heart?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block L-type Ca2+ channels in both blood vessels and the heart, causing vasodilation plus slowing of the SA/AV node (negative chronotropy) and reduced contractility (negative inotropy).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the main indications for rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil/diltiazem)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rate control in AF/SVT, angina (including when a beta-blocker is contraindicated), and less commonly hypertension.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must verapamil or diltiazem never be combined with a beta-blocker?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive AV-node block can cause severe bradycardia, complete heart block or asystole. This is the classic dangerous combination to avoid.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key contraindications to rate-limiting CCBs (verapamil/diltiazem)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 2nd/3rd degree AV block or significant bradycardia, heart failure with reduced EF (negative inotropy causes decompensation), and concurrent beta-blocker use. Also avoid in VT and WPW with AF.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the common and important side effects of verapamil and diltiazem?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bradycardia and AV block, constipation (especially verapamil - very common), and worsening heart failure with ankle oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the important drug interactions with verapamil and diltiazem (besides beta-blockers)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Verapamil raises digoxin levels (toxicity risk), and both raise simvastatin levels - limit simvastatin to a maximum of 20 mg/day (MHRA advice).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring is needed for patients on verapamil or diltiazem?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor HR, BP and ECG for AV conduction, especially if co-prescribed with digoxin or a beta-blocker.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical starting/dose regimen for verapamil in AF rate control?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Verapamil 40-120 mg TDS (or modified-release once daily).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the key distinction between verapamil and diltiazem?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Verapamil is the most negatively inotropic (most constipation, avoid in heart failure), whereas diltiazem is intermediate (rate control plus vasodilation) and better tolerated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: how do they lower blood pressure and slow the heart? (mechanism)
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block beta-1 adrenoceptors (mainly cardiac), reducing heart rate, contractility and AV conduction -> lower cardiac output and BP. They also reduce renin release.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what are the main indications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure with reduced EF (prognostic), angina, post-MI secondary prevention, AF/arrhythmia rate control, and hypertension (step-4 add-on, not first-line unless another indication is present).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: which three improve survival in heart failure, and how should they be started?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol. Start low, go slow, and only when the patient is stable; expect transient early worsening as you uptitrate.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what are the key contraindications/cautions?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Asthma (beta-2 blockade -> bronchospasm; relative CI, use a cardioselective agent with caution only if unavoidable), severe bradycardia or 2nd/3rd degree heart block, decompensated heart failure, and cardiogenic shock.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what are the common and important side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bradycardia, fatigue/lethargy, cold peripheries, bronchospasm, erectile dysfunction, and vivid dreams/nightmares (lipophilic agents). They also mask the tachycardia that warns of hypoglycaemia in diabetics.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: which drug interaction is dangerous and must be avoided?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Never combine with verapamil or diltiazem -> additive AV block causing severe bradycardia, heart block or asystole. NSAIDs blunt the antihypertensive effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: why must you never stop them abruptly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia, angina or MI. Always taper the dose down.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: typical bisoprolol dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Bisoprolol 1.25-2.5 mg once daily, titrated up to 10 mg in heart failure (hypertension max 20 mg OD); start low.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: which is the classic 'non-cardiac' beta-blocker and what is it used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Propranolol (non-selective, lipophilic) -> used for thyrotoxicosis, anxiety/tremor, essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis and portal hypertension (variceal bleed prophylaxis). Avoid in asthma.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what makes carvedilol useful in heart failure and what is its trade-off?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Carvedilol adds alpha-1 blockade (vasodilation, reduces afterload) to beta-blockade. But it is non-selective, so worse in asthma and can cause a postural drop, especially with the first dose.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Beta-blockers: what is notable about atenolol?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Water-soluble (hydrophilic) -> renally cleared (reduce dose in CKD) with poor CNS penetration (fewer nightmares). No longer favoured for hypertension due to weaker stroke-prevention evidence.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics lower blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule causing mild natriuresis; long-term the main BP effect is reduced peripheral vascular resistance.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Where do thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics sit in the NICE hypertension pathway, and which type is preferred?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Used as a step 3 add-on in hypertension. A thiazide-LIKE diuretic (e.g. indapamide) is preferred over a classic thiazide (e.g. bendroflumethiazide).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical starting dose of indapamide for hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Indapamide 2.5 mg once daily.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key contraindications/cautions for thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Avoid in gout/hyperuricaemia (they raise urate and trigger attacks), hyponatraemia or hypokalaemia, and Addison's; caution in diabetes (raise glucose).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the classic electrolyte and metabolic side effects of thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Low K+ and low Na+ (classic - check U&Es), plus HIGH calcium, urate (-> gout), glucose and lipids. Also postural hypotension and erectile dysfunction.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drug interactions matter for thiazide/thiazide-like diuretics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: NSAIDs blunt the effect and risk AKI; lithium excretion falls -> lithium toxicity; loop diuretics/steroids add to hypokalaemia which increases digoxin toxicity risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring is needed when starting a thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es (Na+ and K+) at baseline and after starting or dose change (they drop both). Check glucose in diabetics and urate if gout-prone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: how do they lower fluid volume / act?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, causing powerful natriuresis and diuresis. They also venodilate, giving rapid relief in pulmonary oedema.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: main indications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Fluid overload - heart failure, pulmonary oedema, and nephrotic or hepatic oedema. They are NOT a first-line antihypertensive (used for BP mainly when heart failure or CKD coexists).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: typical starting dose of furosemide?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Furosemide 40 mg OD PO (range 20-80 mg); give IV in acute pulmonary oedema. Bumetanide 1 mg is roughly equivalent to furosemide 40 mg.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: key contraindications and cautions?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Avoid in severe hypokalaemia/hyponatraemia, dehydration/hypovolaemia and anuria. Caution in gout, hepatic encephalopathy, prostatic enlargement/urinary retention, and severe sulfonamide allergy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: important side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypomagnesaemia and hypocalcaemia (they lose Ca2+, opposite of thiazides), plus hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Also dehydration/AKI, hyperuricaemia (gout), hyperglycaemia and ototoxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: what causes ototoxicity?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: High-dose or rapid IV administration - so give IV doses slowly. Remember thiazides retain calcium whereas loops lose it.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the dangerous drug interactions with loop diuretics?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Aminoglycosides -> additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; digoxin -> loop-induced hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin toxicity; lithium -> reduced excretion causing lithium toxicity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: essential monitoring?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: U&Es (especially K+ and Na+) and renal function, as loops drop K+ and can cause AKI if over-diuresed. Use daily weights in acute heart failure to guide diuresis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Loop diuretics: why choose bumetanide over furosemide in some patients?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Furosemide has variable oral absorption that worsens when the gut is oedematous; bumetanide has better, more predictable oral absorption in gut oedema (1 mg ≈ 40 mg furosemide).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Potassium-sparing diuretics / aldosterone antagonists: how do they lower BP and affect potassium?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Spironolactone and eplerenone block the mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) receptor in the distal nephron, causing mild loss of Na+ and water while retaining K+ (potassium-sparing). Amiloride and triamterene do the same by blocking the epithelial Na+ channel (ENaC), independent of aldosterone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone/eplerenone): main clinical uses?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure with reduced EF (improves survival, added to an ACEi and beta-blocker), resistant hypertension as NICE step 4, primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), and ascites in cirrhosis (spironolactone first-line).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Resistant hypertension: when is spironolactone added as NICE step 4?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Add spironolactone as step 4 only if serum K+ is 4.5 or below (because of the risk of hyperkalaemia). If K+ is higher, an alternative such as a further diuretic or an alpha/beta-blocker is used instead.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Aldosterone antagonists: main danger and key side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia is the key danger (can cause fatal arrhythmia) and can precipitate AKI. Spironolactone also causes gynaecomastia, breast tenderness and menstrual upset from off-target sex-hormone effects.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Spironolactone vs eplerenone: the key practical distinction?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Spironolactone is non-selective and commonly causes gynaecomastia; eplerenone is selective so causes far less. If a patient develops breast effects on spironolactone, switch to eplerenone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Aldosterone antagonists: contraindications?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hyperkalaemia (K+ above 5.0), severe renal impairment, and Addison's disease. Use with caution when combined with an ACEi or ARB unless K+ is monitored closely.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Aldosterone antagonists: important drug interactions causing hyperkalaemia?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive hyperkalaemia with ACEi/ARBs, K+ supplements, trimethoprim and NSAIDs, so monitor K+ closely. Spironolactone can also raise digoxin levels.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Aldosterone antagonists: essential monitoring?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es (K+ and creatinine) before starting, at about 1 week and 1 month, then periodically. Stop the drug if K+ rises above 6.0 or the patient develops AKI.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Spironolactone: typical starting dose in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 25 mg once daily (range 12.5-50 mg). Higher doses (up to 100-400 mg) are used for ascites in cirrhosis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Amiloride and triamterene (ENaC blockers): what are they used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are weak diuretics used mainly as a potassium-sparing add-on to a thiazide or loop diuretic to offset K+ loss (e.g. co-amilofruse). Main risk is hyperkalaemia, so check U&Es.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: how do they lower blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They block alpha-1 adrenoceptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and a fall in BP. They also relax prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle, improving urinary flow.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: where do they sit in hypertension therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They are used for resistant hypertension, added at NICE step 4 when K+ is >4.5 (e.g. doxazosin).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the other main indication besides hypertension?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), where they relax bladder-neck smooth muscle to improve urinary flow; tamsulosin is uroselective and used mainly for this.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the characteristic side effect and how do you avoid it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: First-dose and postural hypotension with dizziness or syncope. Give the first dose at bedtime, and use modified-release doxazosin to smooth the postural drop.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: name other important side effects.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dizziness, headache, ankle oedema, and urinary incontinence (in women).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what cautions should you consider before prescribing?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Caution with postural hypotension, in the elderly (falls risk), and in patients with existing urinary incontinence.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what are the key drug interactions?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil) and other antihypertensives cause additive hypotension -> start low and separate dosing. Do not co-prescribe two alpha-blockers.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what monitoring is needed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check lying and standing (postural) BP, especially after the first dose and after each dose increase.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Alpha-blockers: what is the typical starting dose of doxazosin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Doxazosin 1 mg once daily, titrated up (modified-release up to 8 mg).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must tamsulosin be flagged to the surgeon before cataract surgery?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Tamsulosin can cause intra-operative floppy iris syndrome -> warn the ophthalmologist before cataract surgery.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How do centrally-acting antihypertensives (methyldopa, moxonidine) lower blood pressure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: They reduce central sympathetic outflow from the brain, which lowers BP. Methyldopa acts as a central alpha-2 agonist; moxonidine is another centrally-acting agent.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the main clinical use of methyldopa?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypertension in pregnancy. It has a long safety record but is not first-line (labetalol is first-line, modified-release nifedipine the usual alternative); methyldopa is used where these are unsuitable.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key contraindications to methyldopa?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Depression (can precipitate or worsen it), active liver disease, and phaeochromocytoma.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the important side effects of methyldopa?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Sedation/drowsiness, depression, dry mouth and postural hypotension. Also Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia and drug-induced hepatitis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring is required for methyldopa?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: LFTs (risk of drug-induced hepatitis) and FBC plus a direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test for haemolytic anaemia, at baseline and periodically.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is methyldopa the go-to antihypertensive in pregnancy, and what are its main side effects?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is the classic hypertension-in-pregnancy drug. Watch for depression, sedation and a positive Coombs test/haemolysis. Stop it postnatally as it worsens postnatal depression.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical starting dose of methyldopa?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 250 mg twice to three times daily (up to a maximum of 3 g/day).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the place in therapy of moxonidine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A later-line option for resistant hypertension, used as an add-on when standard agents are unsuitable or insufficient.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must moxonidine not be stopped abruptly?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension, so it must be tapered. If the patient is also on a beta-blocker, stop the moxonidine first. Monitor HR and BP.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the four Vaughan-Williams classes of antiarrhythmics, with one example of each?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Class I = Na+ channel blockers (e.g. flecainide); Class II = beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol); Class III = K+ channel blockers (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol); Class IV = rate-limiting non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers (e.g. verapamil, diltiazem).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How are the Class I antiarrhythmics subdivided (Ia/Ib/Ic)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ia (e.g. quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) moderately block Na+ and also block K+ -> widen QRS and prolong QT. Ib (e.g. lidocaine, mexiletine) act selectively on ventricle and shorten the action potential (no QT effect). Ic (e.g. flecainide, propafenone) potently block Na+ -> markedly widen QRS with little effect on QT.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is flecainide (Class Ic) used for and in whom?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rhythm control of paroxysmal AF (including 'pill-in-the-pocket') and SVT (AVNRT/AVRT) - but only in structurally normal hearts. Typical dose 50-100 mg BD; pill-in-the-pocket 200-300 mg as a single PRN dose.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must flecainide (Class Ic) be avoided in structural or ischaemic heart disease?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is proarrhythmic in this setting and increases mortality (CAST trial) - so avoid after MI, in heart failure or LV impairment. Screen for structural disease (often an echo) before starting.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must flecainide always be co-prescribed with an AV-nodal blocker in AF or atrial flutter?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: By slowing the atrial rate it can allow 1:1 AV conduction, producing a dangerously fast ventricular rate. Always pair it with a beta-blocker or rate-limiting CCB (verapamil/diltiazem).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does amiodarone interact with flecainide, and what must you do?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Amiodarone raises flecainide levels -> halve the flecainide dose. Flecainide itself raises digoxin levels.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is lidocaine (Class Ib) used for as an antiarrhythmic, and how is it given?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: IV for ventricular arrhythmias (VT), classically ischaemic/post-MI, as second-line to amiodarone. It must be given IV (heavy first-pass), preferentially acting on depolarised/ischaemic ventricular tissue and not affecting the QT.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the characteristic toxicity of lidocaine, and when is dose reduction needed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dose-related CNS toxicity: perioral/tongue tingling, light-headedness, slurred speech, confusion, twitching -> seizures; high doses cause myocardial depression and hypotension. Reduce the dose in hepatic impairment and heart failure (reduced clearance).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the signature toxicities of the Class Ia drugs (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Class-wide QT prolongation -> torsades/proarrhythmia. Quinidine -> cinchonism (tinnitus, headache, visual upset, GI) and thrombocytopenia; procainamide -> drug-induced lupus and agranulocytosis; disopyramide -> anticholinergic effects and negative inotropy (can precipitate heart failure). These drugs are largely historical.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does amiodarone (Class III) work?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Mainly blocks K+ channels, prolonging repolarisation and refractoriness (lengthens the action potential and QT). It also has Class I, II and IV actions, making it very broad-spectrum.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What arrhythmias is amiodarone used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Broad-spectrum: AF rhythm control, VT/VF, and refractory arrhythmias. Also used in cardiac arrest with shockable rhythms (VF/pulseless VT).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is amiodarone often chosen over flecainide for AF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is safe in structural heart disease and heart failure, where flecainide is unsafe/contraindicated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the contraindications and cautions for amiodarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Caution/avoid in thyroid disease, severe hepatic impairment, severe conduction disturbance or sinoatrial disease (unless paced), and iodine sensitivity.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why does amiodarone have a ~50-day half-life and need loading?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is highly lipophilic with a huge volume of distribution (~60 L/kg), loading into fat, liver, lung and myocardium. This gives slow onset (so it needs loading) and a terminal half-life of weeks to months, meaning effects and interactions persist long after stopping.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical oral loading and maintenance regimen for amiodarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Oral loading 200 mg TDS for 1 week, then 200 mg BD for 1 week, then 200 mg OD maintenance. In VF/pulseless VT arrest, give 300 mg IV (central line preferred).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the classic multi-organ toxicity of amiodarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Thyroid (hypo- or hyperthyroidism, as it is iodine-rich), pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, corneal microdeposits (visual halos, reversible), optic neuropathy (can cause blindness), slate-grey skin with photosensitivity, peripheral neuropathy, and QT prolongation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why does amiodarone cause thyroid problems?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is iodine-rich, which can cause either hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which amiodarone eye effect is dangerous and requires withdrawal?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Optic neuropathy/neuritis can cause blindness and requires stopping the drug (MHRA warning). Corneal microdeposits causing visual halos are common but benign and reversible.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key drug interactions with amiodarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It potentiates warfarin (INR rises, reduce warfarin dose) and raises digoxin levels (halve the digoxin dose). It also raises statin levels (myopathy) and adds to other QT-prolongers, risking torsades.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring is required for amiodarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Baseline and 6-monthly TFTs and LFTs, plus baseline CXR (lung fibrosis) and U&Es. Arrange eye review if visual symptoms, and warn about photosensitivity (advise sunblock).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does sotalol work as an antiarrhythmic?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dual action: a non-selective beta-blocker (class II) plus potassium-channel block (class III). It slows the heart rate and prolongs repolarisation, which lengthens the QT interval.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What arrhythmias is sotalol used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rhythm control of AF and treatment of ventricular arrhythmias. A typical regimen is 80 mg BD, up-titrated with ECG checks.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the defining danger of sotalol?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: QT prolongation leading to torsades de pointes. It is dose/level-dependent and made worse by low K+ or Mg2+.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When should sotalol be avoided (contraindications)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Prolonged/congenital long QT, hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia, significant renal impairment (it is renally excreted and accumulates), asthma, and severe bradycardia or heart block.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring does sotalol require?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: ECG/QTc at baseline and after each dose change (stop if QTc excessively prolonged), U&Es to keep K+ and Mg2+ replete, and renal function for dose adjustment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drug interactions increase torsades risk with sotalol?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Additive QT prolongation with other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, macrolides, antipsychotics), and diuretics that cause hypokalaemia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does dronedarone work, and how does it compare to amiodarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is a non-iodinated amiodarone analogue with the same multi-class (I-IV) actions, prolonging repolarisation. Removing the iodine greatly reduces thyroid/lung toxicity but at the cost of efficacy - 'amiodarone without the iodine'.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is dronedarone used for, and at what dose?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rhythm control of non-permanent AF in selected patients to maintain sinus rhythm. Dose is 400 mg BD with food.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When is dronedarone contraindicated?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Heart failure/LV systolic dysfunction (increased mortality) and permanent AF (increased cardiovascular events) - both must be avoided. Also severe hepatic impairment and QT prolongation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the important side effects of dronedarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: GI upset, raised creatinine (from blocked tubular creatinine secretion, not true renal injury), rare severe hepatotoxicity, and QT prolongation. It causes far less thyroid/lung toxicity than amiodarone.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What monitoring and key interactions matter with dronedarone?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Monitor LFTs (baseline and periodic; stop if hepatotoxicity), ECG, and check the AF has not become permanent. It raises digoxin and statin levels, and should not be combined with other QT-prolonging drugs.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does adenosine work as an antiarrhythmic?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It briefly activates A1 receptors in the AV node, causing a few seconds of AV block (transient asystole). This interrupts re-entry circuits that pass through the AV node, terminating the SVT.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is adenosine used for, and what must be tried first?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stable, regular narrow-complex SVT (AVNRT/AVRT), used after vagal manoeuvres (e.g. modified Valsalva, or carotid sinus massage if no bruit/TIA history) have failed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the adenosine dosing regimen for SVT?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 6 mg rapid IV push into a large/proximal vein followed by a fast saline flush -> 12 mg after 1-2 min if no response -> 18 mg after a further 1-2 min if still no response.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why must adenosine be given as a rapid bolus with a fast saline flush?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Its half-life is only seconds (~10 s), so it must reach the heart quickly before being broken down. A large proximal vein plus a fast flush ensures enough drug reaches the AV node to work.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the typical transient side effects of adenosine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A brief impending 'sense of doom'/chest tightness, flushing, dyspnoea and a few seconds of asystole. Warn the patient beforehand that it is unpleasant but passes within seconds.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is adenosine contraindicated in asthma/COPD, and what is the alternative?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It can cause bronchospasm. Use verapamil instead (a rate-limiting CCB) for a confirmed regular narrow-complex SVT - but only if the patient is not on a beta-blocker and has no pre-excitation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Besides asthma, when should adenosine be avoided?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: In 2nd/3rd degree heart block or sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What key drug interactions affect adenosine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dipyridamole potentiates its effect (reduce the dose). Theophylline and caffeine are adenosine antagonists and blunt its effect.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How should adenosine be monitored, and why is this diagnostically useful?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Give under continuous ECG with a rhythm strip recorded and resuscitation facilities to hand. The transient AV block can be diagnostic - slowing the rate unmasks atrial flutter waves.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: A patient in SVT is haemodynamically unstable (shock, syncope, ischaemia, severe HF). Is adenosine appropriate?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: No. An unstable patient needs synchronised DC cardioversion, not adenosine.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does digoxin work (mechanism)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase, so intracellular Na+ rises and less Ca2+ is extruded by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. The resulting rise in intracellular Ca2+ increases the force of contraction (positive inotropy).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does digoxin slow the heart rate?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It increases vagal tone (and reduces sympathetic drive), which slows conduction through the AV node and gives rate control in AF.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the main uses of digoxin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Rate control in AF (best in sedentary or heart-failure patients, poor for exertional rate) and heart failure, where it gives symptom benefit but no prognostic/survival benefit.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is digoxin a poor choice for rate control in an active, exercising patient with AF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Its rate-slowing works mainly through vagal tone, which is overridden by sympathetic drive on exertion, so it controls resting but not exertional heart rate.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the key pharmacological warning about digoxin's dosing?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It has a narrow therapeutic index, so small changes in level or electrolytes can tip a patient from therapeutic into toxic effects.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the cautions/contraindications for digoxin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Caution in renal impairment (renally excreted, so it accumulates), hypokalaemia (potentiates toxicity), and heart block. Contraindicated in WPW/accessory-pathway AF and in VT/VF.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical digoxin regimen, including loading?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 125-250 microgram OD (lower in the elderly or renal impairment). If rapid AF control is needed, load with ~0.75-1.5 mg orally in divided doses over 24 h (e.g. 500 microgram, then 500 microgram 6 h later, then 250 microgram).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the features of digoxin toxicity?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Nausea/vomiting, confusion, xanthopsia (yellow-green vision), and arrhythmias (bradycardia or VT).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which electrolyte disturbance classically precipitates digoxin toxicity, and why does it matter for level interpretation?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Hypokalaemia (also hypomagnesaemia and renal impairment) precipitates toxicity. Because of this, toxicity can occur even when the digoxin level is within range, so a normal level does not exclude it.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the difference between 'digoxin effect' and digoxin toxicity on ECG?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: The therapeutic 'digoxin effect' is a reverse-tick / down-sloping ST segment and is normal. It does not indicate toxicity, which instead presents with arrhythmias and clinical features.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs interact with digoxin and how should you respond?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Loop/thiazide diuretics cause hypokalaemia and precipitate toxicity. Amiodarone, verapamil and quinine raise digoxin levels, so reduce the digoxin dose.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How is digoxin monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Check U&Es (K+, Mg2+ and renal function drive toxicity). Therapeutic level is 0.5-2 microgram/L (aim 0.7-2 in HF/AF), sampled at least 6 h post-dose, remembering the level alone does not exclude toxicity if hypokalaemic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the antidote for life-threatening digoxin toxicity?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab / Digibind).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the first-line drug treatment for chronic stable angina (for symptom control)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: A beta-blocker OR a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker (e.g. verapamil/diltiazem). Choose one first-line for prophylaxis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: In chronic stable angina, what do you do if a single first-line antianginal is insufficient?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Combine a beta-blocker with a dihydropyridine CCB (e.g. amlodipine). Do NOT combine a beta-blocker with a rate-limiting CCB like verapamil.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: In stable angina, what are the options if a beta-blocker plus a dihydropyridine CCB still does not control symptoms?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Add one of: a long-acting nitrate, nicorandil, ivabradine, or ranolazine.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Besides symptom control, what secondary prevention should every patient with angina receive?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Aspirin (antiplatelet), a statin, and an ACE inhibitor where indicated, plus a GTN spray for acute attacks.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) relieve angina?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is a nitric oxide donor causing mainly venodilation -> reduced preload -> reduced myocardial wall tension and oxygen demand; it also dilates coronary arteries and relieves spasm.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is GTN not given orally, and which routes are used instead?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Oral GTN is inactivated by extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism. Sublingual spray/tablet, buccal, IV and transdermal routes bypass this.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is GTN (short-acting) used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: To abort an acute angina attack or taken before predictable exertion. IV infusion is used in ACS, acute LV failure/pulmonary oedema and hypertensive emergencies.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is a typical GTN spray dose for an acute angina attack?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: 1-2 sprays (400 mcg each) sublingually PRN, repeated once after 5 minutes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the GTN rule that patients must be counselled on?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Take a dose; if pain persists, repeat after 5 minutes; if pain is still present 5 minutes after the second dose, call 999.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the most common side effect of GTN and nitrates, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Headache (throbbing) from cerebral vasodilation - it is expected. Also flushing.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What cardiovascular side effects can nitrates cause besides headache?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Postural hypotension, dizziness/syncope and reflex tachycardia.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which drugs are absolutely contraindicated with nitrates (GTN or long-acting), and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) -> profound, potentially fatal hypotension/collapse. Never co-administer.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: In which cardiac conditions should nitrates be avoided?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Severe aortic stenosis and HOCM (preload-dependent -> collapse), plus existing hypotension and raised intracranial pressure.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What practical point should patients know about GTN tablet shelf-life?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: GTN tablets expire about 8 weeks after opening the bottle; the spray lasts longer.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are long-acting nitrates (isosorbide mono-/dinitrate) used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Angina prophylaxis (regular background prevention), not for aborting acute attacks. Same NO-donor/venodilation mechanism as GTN.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is nitrate tolerance and how is it prevented?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Continuous nitrate exposure blunts the effect within ~24 hours. Prevent it with a daily nitrate-free interval of about 10-14 hours.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How is isosorbide mononitrate dosed to provide a nitrate-free interval?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Asymmetric dosing, e.g. 10-40 mg at 8 am and 2 pm, or a modified-release 60 mg once daily formulation that gives an automatic trough.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which oral long-acting nitrate is preferred for prophylaxis and why (student level)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) - it has essentially complete oral bioavailability and a longer duration, making it a reliable oral prophylactic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does nicorandil relieve angina (mechanism)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Dual action: it activates K-ATP channels causing arterial dilation (-> reduced afterload) and has a nitrate moiety causing venodilation (-> reduced preload), giving a balanced reduction in cardiac work.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Where does nicorandil sit in angina treatment?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: An add-on / later-line (second- to third-line) drug for angina, used when a beta-blocker or calcium-channel blocker is insufficient or contraindicated, often while awaiting or unsuitable for revascularisation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the characteristic examinable side effect of nicorandil?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Ulceration of skin and mucosa (oral, anal, perianal, genital, peristomal, GI, ocular). It can be severe, mimic malignancy, and progress to fistula, perforation or haemorrhage.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How should nicorandil-induced ulceration be managed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Stop the drug (do not dose-reduce or treat topically); the ulcers then heal. Also expect headache (common early), flushing and dizziness as other side effects.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which key drug interaction is contraindicated with nicorandil, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) are contraindicated because nicorandil's nitrate moiety causes profound hypotension - the same contraindication as GTN/nitrates.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does ivabradine work in angina?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It selectively inhibits the funny current (I_f) in the SA node, slowing the sinus rate. This reduces myocardial oxygen demand without affecting BP, contractility or AV conduction ('pure' heart-rate reduction).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: When is ivabradine used, and what rhythm is required?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: For chronic stable angina (resting HR >=70 bpm) and symptomatic HFrEF (EF <=35%, HR >=75 bpm), usually when intolerant of or maximally treated with a beta-blocker. It works ONLY in sinus rhythm.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Why is ivabradine ineffective and contraindicated in atrial fibrillation?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It acts on the SA node's funny current, so it only slows the rate in sinus rhythm. In AF the SA node is not driving the rhythm, so it does not work and is contraindicated.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the signature side effect of ivabradine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Luminous visual phenomena (phosphenes) - transient brightness or halos, in about 15% of patients. They are harmless and arise from the same funny-current channels in the retina.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What are the key contraindications and cautions for ivabradine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Atrial fibrillation, significant bradycardia / sick sinus / heart block, acute coronary syndrome, severe hypotension or cardiogenic shock, and severe hepatic impairment. Also avoid with drugs that raise its levels (e.g. verapamil, diltiazem) and with grapefruit juice.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How is ivabradine dosed and monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Start 5 mg BD (2.5 mg BD in elderly), titrate to 7.5 mg BD by heart rate. If resting HR falls <50 bpm or symptomatic bradycardia occurs, reduce to 2.5 mg BD or stop.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does ranolazine relieve angina, and what is special about its haemodynamic effect?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It inhibits the late inward sodium current, reducing sodium-driven calcium overload and improving myocardial relaxation and perfusion. Crucially, it does NOT change heart rate or BP, so it is useful when these are already low.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Where does ranolazine sit in the treatment of stable angina?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is an add-on for chronic stable angina when other antianginals are insufficient or not tolerated - particularly helpful when HR and BP are already low and cannot be lowered further.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the signature side effect and key monitoring requirement for ranolazine?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: QT prolongation is the signature concern. Monitor the ECG for QT, and avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs (additive effect). It is contraindicated in existing QT prolongation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: How does trimetazidine work as an antianginal?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It is a metabolic modulator: it shifts myocardial energy production toward more oxygen-efficient glucose oxidation, giving an anti-anginal effect with no haemodynamic (HR/BP) change.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: What is the signature caution with trimetazidine, and where does it sit in therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: It can cause or worsen drug-induced parkinsonism, tremor and movement disorders (usually reversible on stopping), so avoid in Parkinson's disease. It is an MHRA-restricted second-line add-on for refractory stable angina only, rarely used in the UK.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.front: Which patient with refractory angina might suit ranolazine or trimetazidine rather than a rate-limiting drug?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Anti.back: Both work without lowering heart rate or blood pressure, so they are useful add-ons when HR and BP are already low. Choose based on cautions: watch QT with ranolazine, and avoid trimetazidine in Parkinson's/movement disorders.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What are the four pillars of HFrEF drug therapy that improve survival?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: (1) An ACE inhibitor or ARB (or ARNI in their place), (2) a beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol or nebivolol), (3) a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone), and (4) an SGLT2 inhibitor. All four are prognostic and are started and up-titrated early together, not in strict sequence.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: In HFrEF, which drugs are prognostic (improve survival) versus symptomatic?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: The four pillars (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i) improve survival. Loop diuretics (furosemide/bumetanide) relieve congestion and symptoms but do NOT improve prognosis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is Pillar 1 of HFrEF therapy and how is it dosed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: An ACE inhibitor (or ARB if ACEi-intolerant due to cough, or an ARNI once stable). Start early in all patients with reduced EF and titrate to the maximum tolerated dose, as benefit is dose-related.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is Pillar 2 of HFrEF therapy, and which agents are used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: A beta-blocker. Only three have HFrEF mortality evidence: bisoprolol, carvedilol and nebivolol. Start only when the patient is stable/euvolaemic, never in acute decompensation.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is Pillar 3 of HFrEF therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) - spironolactone or eplerenone - added to ACEi/ARNI plus a beta-blocker in symptomatic HFrEF. It is prognostic (improves survival).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is Pillar 4 of HFrEF therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: An SGLT2 inhibitor. It is a prognostic pillar that reduces mortality and heart failure hospitalisation in HFrEF.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is the role of loop diuretics (furosemide/bumetanide) in HFrEF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: They relieve congestion and symptoms (oedema, breathlessness, pulmonary oedema) but do NOT improve prognosis. Use the lowest dose that keeps the patient euvolaemic.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: When is ivabradine or digoxin used as an add-on in HFrEF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Ivabradine is an add-on for patients in sinus rhythm with heart rate >=75. Digoxin is a symptomatic add-on (improves symptoms, not prognosis).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: When is hydralazine plus a nitrate used in HFrEF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: As an alternative for patients intolerant of ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and as an add-on in Black patients.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: How do SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) work in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: They block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, causing glycosuria and natriuresis/osmotic diuresis. This reduces preload/afterload and improves myocardial energetics, giving cardiorenal benefit that is independent of diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is the place of SGLT2 inhibitors in HFrEF therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: They are the fourth pillar of HFrEF treatment. They are prognostic - reducing HF hospitalisation and cardiovascular death regardless of whether the patient has diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: Besides heart failure, what other conditions are SGLT2 inhibitors used for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (they are renoprotective). In HF their benefit applies even without diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is the typical dose of dapagliflozin/empagliflozin in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: 10 mg once daily - a flat dose with no titration needed.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What are the key side effects of SGLT2 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Genital/urinary infections (thrush) from glycosuria, volume depletion, euglycaemic DKA (DKA with near-normal glucose), and rarely Fournier's gangrene.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What should you do about the small early eGFR dip seen after starting an SGLT2 inhibitor?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: A small early drop in eGFR is expected and reversible - do not stop the drug for it. Continue to monitor renal function.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What sick-day rule should patients on SGLT2 inhibitors be counselled on?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Hold the drug if unwell, dehydrated, or not eating, to reduce the risk of volume depletion and euglycaemic DKA.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What does ARNI stand for, and what are the two components of sacubitril/valsartan?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Angiotensin Receptor-Neprilysin Inhibitor. It combines valsartan (an ARB that blocks the AT1 receptor) with sacubitril (a neprilysin inhibitor).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: How does sacubitril (the neprilysin inhibitor in ARNI) help in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: It stops the breakdown of natriuretic peptides, leading to vasodilation, natriuresis, and anti-remodelling. Valsartan simultaneously blocks the harmful effects of angiotensin II.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is the role of sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) in HFrEF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: It REPLACES the ACEi/ARB in HFrEF patients who remain symptomatic on optimal therapy (or as an early alternative to an ACEi). It improves survival (prognostic), based on PARADIGM-HF where it was superior to an ACEi.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: Why must you wait 36 hours after stopping an ACEi before starting sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: To avoid angioedema. Both ACEi and ARNI raise bradykinin, so a 36-hour washout is the critical safety step before starting.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What are the key contraindications to sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Pregnancy, prior ACEi/ARB-related or hereditary/idiopathic angioedema (absolute), starting within 36 h of an ACEi, severe hepatic impairment, and K+ >5.4.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What are the important side effects of sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Hypotension (common - the main limiter of uptitration), hyperkalaemia, renal impairment, and angioedema (higher risk in Black patients).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: How is response to therapy monitored on sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI), and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Use NT-proBNP, not BNP. Neprilysin inhibition raises BNP (a neprilysin substrate) so BNP becomes uninterpretable, whereas NT-proBNP still falls with genuine improvement. Also monitor U&Es and BP after starting and each uptitration.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is a typical starting and target dose of sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Start 49/51 mg BD and uptitrate to 97/103 mg BD. Start lower at 24/26 mg BD if low BP, on a low ACEi dose, or renal impairment.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: How does the hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate combination help in heart failure (simple mechanism)?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Hydralazine is a direct arterial vasodilator -> reduces afterload; isosorbide dinitrate is a venodilator -> reduces preload. Together they offload the failing heart.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is the role of hydralazine + nitrate in HFrEF?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: An alternative for patients who cannot take an ACEi/ARB/ARNI (e.g. renal impairment or hyperkalaemia), and an add-on in Black patients with persistent symptoms despite optimal therapy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: Which drug class is contraindicated with the nitrate component of hydralazine + ISDN, and why?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: PDE5 inhibitors (e.g. sildenafil) -> risk of severe hypotension when combined with nitrates.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is the signature side effect of hydralazine, and how is it monitored?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Drug-induced lupus (dose-related and reversible). Check ANA if the patient develops arthralgia or rash, especially with higher-dose/long-term use.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.front: What is a typical dose of the hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate combination in heart failure?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Hear.back: Hydralazine 25-75 mg QDS plus isosorbide dinitrate 20-40 mg TDS (a fixed-dose combination is available).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the mechanism of action of statins?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis. The liver responds by upregulating LDL receptors, which clears LDL from the blood.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Besides lowering LDL, what pleiotropic benefit do statins provide?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They stabilise atherosclerotic plaques and improve endothelial function.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: For primary prevention of cardiovascular disease, which statin and dose is first-line, and at what threshold?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Atorvastatin 20 mg once daily, offered when QRISK3 is >=10%.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Name two groups who should be offered a statin for primary prevention regardless of their QRISK3 score.
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: People with type 1 diabetes and people with chronic kidney disease. A statin is also considered in those aged >=85 years.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: For secondary prevention (post-MI, ischaemic stroke, or peripheral arterial disease), which statin and dose is used?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Atorvastatin 80 mg once daily (high-intensity).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: A patient has suspected familial hypercholesterolaemia. How does management differ from ordinary primary prevention?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: QRISK does NOT apply. Refer to a specialist and arrange cascade testing of family members. Typical features are very high LDL, tendon xanthomata, and premature cardiovascular disease.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: When during the day should atorvastatin versus simvastatin be taken?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Atorvastatin (20 or 80 mg) can be taken at any time of day. Simvastatin should be dosed at night.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the two key contraindications to starting a statin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Pregnancy or breastfeeding (cholesterol is needed for fetal development, so stop the statin), and active liver disease / persistent transaminitis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the most common muscle-related side effect of statins, and how common is it?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Myalgia/myopathy is a common patient complaint. Most muscle aches are benign, but they must be distinguished from rare serious myopathy.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: A patient on a statin has severe muscle pain and dark urine. What is the concern and what do you do?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Rhabdomyolysis. Check creatine kinase (CK) and stop the statin.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How is a mild rise in ALT on a statin managed, and when should you stop the drug?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: A mild transaminitis is common and a rise of less than 3x the upper limit of normal is NOT a reason to stop. Stop the statin if ALT rises to more than 3x ULN.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What metabolic side effect can statins cause?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: A small excess of new-onset type 2 diabetes. (Also GI upset and headache.) The cardiovascular benefit still outweighs this risk.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Simvastatin dose is capped at a maximum of 20 mg when co-prescribed with which drugs?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Amlodipine, diltiazem, verapamil, or amiodarone (these raise simvastatin levels and increase myopathy risk).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Which drugs should make you AVOID simvastatin altogether?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Clarithromycin/erythromycin, azole antifungals, HIV protease inhibitors, ciclosporin, and gemfibrozil.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: A patient on simvastatin is prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection. What is the practical action?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Hold (stop) the statin for the duration of the antibiotic course, then restart afterwards.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Why is gemfibrozil contraindicated with any statin, and what is the alternative if a fibrate is needed?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: The combination markedly increases the risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis. If a fibrate is required, fenofibrate is preferred.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Which common dietary item, in large amounts, raises statin levels?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Grapefruit (in large quantities).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the LFT monitoring schedule for a patient starting a statin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Check LFTs at baseline, 3 months, and 12 months, then not routinely. A rise of less than 3x ULN is not a reason to stop.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How is the lipid response to a statin monitored, and what is the target?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Check lipids / non-HDL cholesterol at baseline and at 3 months, aiming for at least a 40% fall in non-HDL cholesterol.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: A patient reports muscle aches on a statin (statin intolerance). Why not simply stop it, and what is the approach?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Don't just stop and give up. Exclude other causes, then stop and rechallenge at a lower dose, alternate-day dosing, or a different statin, before moving to an alternative such as ezetimibe.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: When should HbA1c be checked in a patient on a statin?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: At baseline and around 3 months in those at risk of diabetes, given the small excess risk of new-onset type 2 diabetes.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How does ezetimibe lower LDL cholesterol?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: It blocks the NPC1L1 cholesterol transporter in the small intestine -> reduces absorption of dietary and biliary cholesterol -> the liver upregulates LDL receptors -> LDL falls by ~15-20%.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: When is ezetimibe used in lipid-lowering therapy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: As the first add-on to a statin when the LDL/non-HDL target isn't reached (gives added cardiovascular benefit). It can be used as monotherapy in patients who are statin-intolerant.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the typical dose of ezetimibe?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Ezetimibe 10 mg orally once daily (can be taken at any time of day).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How well tolerated is ezetimibe, and what side effects can occur?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Generally very well tolerated. Occasionally causes GI upset or myalgia, and (when combined with a statin) a small rise in transaminases.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How should ezetimibe be timed relative to a bile-acid sequestrant?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Bile-acid sequestrants reduce ezetimibe absorption -> give ezetimibe at least 2 hours before, or at least 4 hours after, the sequestrant.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How do PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) lower LDL?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They are monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9. PCSK9 normally tags LDL receptors for destruction, so blocking it means more LDL receptors are recycled to the cell surface -> a large LDL fall (~50-60%) on top of a statin.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Who are PCSK9 inhibitors reserved for?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They are a specialist add-on for familial hypercholesterolaemia, or for established cardiovascular disease with persistently high LDL despite a maximal statin plus ezetimibe (used at NICE thresholds).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How are PCSK9 inhibitors given?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: By subcutaneous injection, e.g. evolocumab every 2 weeks (or once monthly). No routine monitoring bloods are required.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What are the main side effects of PCSK9 inhibitors?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Injection-site reactions and flu-like symptoms. Otherwise very well tolerated, with no myopathy signal (unlike statins).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Can PCSK9 inhibitors be used in pregnancy?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: No - avoid in pregnancy and breast-feeding due to limited safety data.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How does inclisiran lower LDL cholesterol?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: It is a small interfering RNA (siRNA) taken up by the liver that silences PCSK9 -> fewer PCSK9 proteins -> more LDL receptors -> a large LDL reduction. It is long-lasting, which allows twice-yearly dosing.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the licensed indication for inclisiran?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Secondary prevention only: established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease with LDL-C persistently >=2.6 mmol/L despite maximal tolerated statin +/- ezetimibe.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the dosing schedule for inclisiran?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Subcutaneous injection at 0 and 3 months, then every 6 months (twice yearly). The infrequent dosing makes it excellent for adherence.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Inclisiran vs PCSK9 antibodies (evolocumab/alirocumab) - how do they compare?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Both act on the same target (PCSK9). The antibodies bind and neutralise the PCSK9 protein and are given every 2-4 weeks; inclisiran is an siRNA that silences PCSK9 production and is given only twice yearly - same target, different modality.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: How do fibrates (e.g. fenofibrate, bezafibrate) work, and what is their main lipid effect?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: They are PPAR-alpha agonists. Their main effect is to lower triglycerides (with a modest rise in HDL).

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: What is the main indication for a fibrate?
pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.back: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia, especially TG >10 mmol/L, to prevent acute pancreatitis.

pharmacology__Cardiovascular Drugs__Lipi.front: Does NICE recommend fibrates for mixed dyslipidaemia or added to a statin for cardiovascular prevention?
